children: China has tightened emissions-intensity benchmarks for most coal-fired power units under its national emissions trading scheme or ETS for 2025-26, while keeping the allocation methodology for the steel, cement and aluminum sectors unchanged from 2025, according to the Ministry of Ecology and Environment notice released Wednesday.

The allocation plan lowers the benchmark for conventional coal-fired units above 300 megawatts to 0.7894 mtCO2/MWh in 2026, from 0.7902 mtCO2/MWh in 2025. The benchmark for conventional coal units of 300 MW or less falls to 0.7985 mtCO2/MWh from 0.8017 mtCO2/MWh, while the benchmark for unconventional coal units drops to 0.8080 mtCO2/MWh from 0.8162 mtCO2/MWh. The gas-fired power benchmark remains unchanged.

The lower benchmarks mean power generators with higher emissions intensity will face greater pressure to improve efficiency, while more efficient plants will be better positioned to generate an allocation surplus. China said the allocation system would continue to prioritize efficiency, with lower-emitting entities receiving higher surplus rates.
Despite the tightening of benchmark values for power sector, The Chinese Emission Allowance or CEA prices have fallen amid profit taking.
CEA was last traded at 94.40 yuan ($13.92) per metric ton on the Shanghai Environment and Energy Exchange on Thursday, which is down 1.05 yuan/mt on day and down 4.12 yuan/mt on week.

By contrast, the allocation methodology for steel, cement, and aluminum--sectors newly added to China's ETS in 2025--remains unchanged. For 2026, these three sectors will continue to receive allowances based on emissions-intensity coefficients rather than the benchmark approach used for power.

Under the industrial-sector methodology, allowances are adjusted according to how a company's emissions intensity compares with the industry balance value. Companies performing better than the benchmark receive a positive adjustment, while those performing worse receive a negative adjustment.
China will continue to provide free allowances and on an intensity-based basis for now, but the government said it would prepare for a future system combining free and paid allocation.

For 2025 and 2026 power-sector allocations and 2026 industrial-sector allocations, initial allowances will generally be set at 50% of the previous year's verified emissions, before being adjusted based on verified emissions for the relevant year. Provincial authorities can lower the initial allocation ratio based on compliance risks and production conditions.
